projects.name: Autonomous Search & Rescue: Frontier Exploration for Quadruped Robots
projects.title: Robotics & Autonomous Systems Engineer
projects.tldr:
• Developed an autonomous exploration framework for the Unitree Go2 quadruped, targeting hazardous, unstructured Search and Rescue (SAR) environments.
  • Implemented a perception pipeline using Bayesian log-odds updates to fuse 3D LiDAR point clouds into filtered 2D occupancy grids for stable mapping.
  • Engineered a custom frontier-based exploration node that autonomously selects mission goals by balancing Euclidean distance against area coverage utility.
  • Leveraged the ROS2 Navigation2 (Nav2) stack and tuned its Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller to achieve smooth navigation through narrow, debris-filled corridors.
  • Bridged high-level ROS2 velocity commands with low-level Unitree API calls to enable seamless, collision-free hardware actuation.
projects.summary:
In Search and Rescue (SAR) sectors—a market projected to reach $15.7 billion by 2031—the challenge is operating in hazardous, unknown environments. Our team developed an open-source autonomous exploration framework for the Unitree Go2 quadruped, fusing complex legged mobility with real-time mapping to navigate three-dimensional obstacles common in disaster sites.

System ArchitecturePerception-to-Actuation Pipeline



Probabilistic Mapping & Awareness

We achieved real-time environment awareness by converting the local 3D LiDAR stream into an accurate 2D occupancy grid. To ensure the map was robust against sensor noise, we implemented Bayesian log-odds updates. We tuned the occupancy probabilities (0.7 for occupied, 0.1 for free) to allow for rapid detection of static obstacles while enabling the map to "forget" dynamic noise. This created a stable foundation for both the global costmap and our autonomous planner.

Managing complex TF tree transformations (Map -> Odom -> Base_Link -> LiDAR)



Autonomous Frontier Exploration

True autonomy required the robot to identify and prioritize unexplored regions. We developed an Explorer Node that scans the occupancy grid for frontiers—boundaries between known free space and unknown territory. We implemented a utility function that selects goals based on the shortest Euclidean distance. To ensure safety, we filtered out frontier candidates located too close to obstacles or in non-traversable regions, biasing the robot toward safe, open-space exploration.

Frontier cells overlaid on the costmap with the selected goal and Nav2 optimal path



Navigation & Control Interface

Once a frontier goal is set, the Nav2 stack handles path execution. We leveraged Nav2’s Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller, which samples thousands of candidate control sequences to optimize for path tracking and obstacle avoidance. We then developed a dedicated cmd_vel_to_go2 node to translate these standard ROS2 velocity commands into the Unitree-specific API calls required to drive the quadruped's motors, completing the perception-planning-actuation loop.

Experimental Results

We validated the system in an unknown maze environment. The robot successfully identified the corridor layout and autonomously navigated to the dead end, updating the occupancy grid in real-time as frontiers were cleared.

Exploration StartFinal Mapping Success



Full closed-loop exploration in the maze environment

Generalizing the exploration pipeline to an open indoor setting



Project Limitations

While the system performed reliably in maze and office environments, we identified several primary areas for future improvement:

  • Frame Drift: In our current setup, the map frame is locked to the odometry (odom) frame. For large-scale environments, this leads to accumulated drift, which could be mitigated by integrating a SLAM back-end for loop closure.
  • Onboard Compute Load: All processing currently runs on the Go2's internal hardware. The high computational demand for real-time 3D-to-2D projection and MPPI sampling suggests that future iterations should explore offboard edge computing to reduce latency.
  • Dynamic Sensitivity: The pipeline is optimized for static environments; if the environment changes significantly during execution, the robot may follow a previously valid but now blocked path until the next costmap update.

projects.name: Dynamic Handstand Robot: Classical vs. Learning-Based Control
projects.title: Reinforcement Learning Engineer
projects.tldr:
• Engineered a high-fidelity expert trajectory for a 7-link humanoid, bridging the gap between kinematic keyframing and physically realizable MuJoCo motion.
  • Developed a synthesis pipeline using "privileged DOFs" (root position and torso pitch) to sketch the global motion before correcting for dynamics.
  • Implemented a physics-validation loop to ensure the reference motion respected ground contact and gravity constraints.
  • Built a custom Gymnasium environment to facilitate state-tracking rewards based on the validated expert qpos and qvel data.
  • Trained a robust neural network policy using PPO, benchmarking it against brittle classical controllers and difficult-to-tune pure RL.
projects.summary:
This project benchmarked three control paradigms—Classical, Reinforcement Learning (RL), and Imitation Learning (IL)—for a dynamic handstand task on a 7-link humanoid. While my team explored classical linearization and pure RL, I took ownership of the Imitation Learning pipeline. I identified that for complex, multi-phase robotics tasks, the primary bottleneck is not the learning algorithm itself, but the synthesis of a physically consistent expert trajectory for the agent to follow.

Classical ControlPure RL7-Link Model



Phase 1: Kinematic Sketching (No Physics)

Generating a handstand trajectory is difficult due to the non-linear transition between walking and planting. I began by creating a "ghost" trajectory in a gravity-free kinematic space. By using privileged degrees of freedom—directly commanding the torso's global position and rotation—I was able to sketch the ideal sequence of walking, crouching, and swinging without the initial struggle of balancing dynamics. This allowed me to prioritize the visual timing and reachability of the motion.

Kinematic trajectory synthesis using privileged DOFs (No Physics)



Phase 2: Physics Validation & Refinement

The core engineering challenge was converting the kinematic "ghost" motion into a physically realizable trajectory. I implemented an iterative validation loop in generate_handstand.py. This involved simulating the trajectory with gravity and collisions enabled to detect ground clipping and momentum mismatches. I developed a fix_ground_clipping algorithm that adjusted the root Z-height and joint angles to ensure the hands and feet made contact correctly, resulting in a validated expert dataset ready for imitation.

Physics-corrected reference motion with gravity and ground contact



Phase 3: Learning & Policy Deployment

With the expert trajectory finalized, training the policy became a matter of robust tracking. I built a custom Gymnasium environment where the agent was rewarded for minimizing the error between its state and the expert's qpos and qvel. Using PPO, the policy learned to generate the necessary joint torques to follow the reference path. This Imitation Learning approach provided a controller that was far smoother than pure RL and much less numerically brittle than the classical controller.

Final IL PolicyPPO Training Reward Convergence

projects.name: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Quadruped Locomotion (Unitree Go1)
projects.title: Reinforcement Learning Engineer
projects.tldr:
• Trained a robust velocity-tracking PPO policy for the Unitree Go1 in MuJoCo, parallelized across 4,096 environments for rapid convergence.
  • Implemented an Asymmetric Actor-Critic architecture, leveraging privileged simulator states (ground-truth contact forces and foot height) to guide a proprioception-only actor.
  • Engineered gait-shaping rewards to solve foot-dragging issues, achieving distinct 0.06m parabolic swing trajectories and stable stance phases.
  • Modeled high-fidelity actuator dynamics, including reflected inertia (6:1 gear ratios) and motor limits, to ensure physically realistic behavior without hardware deployment.
  • Conducted comparative analysis on the impact of privileged information, demonstrating significantly reduced tracking error spikes and improved traction.
projects.summary:
This project focused on training a high-performance locomotion controller for the Unitree Go1 quadruped using Deep Reinforcement Learning (PPO). The primary challenge was not just making the robot walk, but ensuring the gait was robust, natural, and physically plausible. By utilizing an Asymmetric Actor-Critic architecture and meticulous reward engineering, I developed a policy capable of tracking omnidirectional velocity commands with high precision.

Final Policy (Gait Shaped)Test-Time Velocity Tracking



Phase 1: Asymmetric Actor-Critic Architecture

To improve training stability, I implemented an Asymmetric Actor-Critic structure. In this setup, the Critic has access to "privileged" simulation data—such as ground-truth foot contact forces, exact foot heights, and friction coefficients—that the Actor (the robot's controller) cannot see. This allows the Critic to learn a more accurate value function, which in turn guides the Actor to learn robust behaviors using only noisy proprioceptive sensors.

Analysis: The inclusion of privileged information significantly reduced the magnitude and frequency of tracking error spikes. As shown below, while both models exhibit similar slip patterns, the improved model exhibits lower peak slip velocities and fewer oscillations. The critic’s access to ground-truth contact data enabled the policy to maintain a more stable, rhythmic gait with better overall traction.

Impact of Privileged Information on Slip Velocity and Tracking Error



Phase 2: Gait Shaping & Trajectory Optimization

Initial policies, while functional, exhibited "shuffling" behavior where the feet barely cleared the ground. To correct this, I engineered specific gait-shaping rewards targeting foot clearance, swing height consistency, and slip penalization.

Analysis: Without gait-shaping rewards, the trajectory was shallow and irregular (approx 0.01m), indicating dragging. In contrast, the improved model produced distinct parabolic arcs reaching approximately 0.06m. This demonstrates a clean lift-off and consistent landing that clearly differentiates between the swing and stance phases.

Before Gait Shaping (Shuffling)After Gait Shaping (Parabolic Arcs)


Foot Trajectory Analysis: Shallow vs. Parabolic Clearance



Phase 3: Training Dynamics & Convergence

The policy was trained across 4,096 parallel environments using MuJoCo's EGL rendering on a T4 GPU. The reward function was designed to prioritize velocity tracking (linear/angular) while regularizing joint torques and action rates to ensure smoothness. The training curves show rapid convergence, with the mean episode length stabilizing quickly, indicating the agent learned to balance and walk without falling early in the training process.

Total Reward ConvergenceMean Episode Length

projects.name: Cassie Bipedal Robot Balance Control
projects.title: Controls Engineer
projects.tldr:
• Implemented a force-control strategy with a PD fallback for the 20-DOF Cassie bipedal robot to maintain balance under external perturbations.
  • Formulated a Quadratic Programming (QP) optimization problem to track a desired COM wrench while respecting frictional and unilateral contact constraints.
  • Achieved a top leaderboard score of 239.96 by implementing a dynamic downward Center of Mass (COM) trajectory to enhance rotational stability.
  • Analyzed the performance trade-offs of real-time solvers like fmincon and the impact of state rotation conventions on system stability.
  • Iteratively tuned the controller to reject significant external force/torque pushes and manage transition phases where contact points were not fully grounded.
projects.summary:
This project focused on developing robust balance control strategies for CASSIE, a bird-inspired 3D bipedal robot with a 20-DOF floating base model. The objective was to design a feedback controller for 10 actuated joint torques to maintain a standing posture while rejecting external pushes and torques.

Force-Control & QP Optimization

The core of the winning submission was a whole-body force-control strategy. Instead of commanding joint positions, I formulated a Quadratic Programming (QP) problem to find the optimal ground reaction forces ($f$) that would generate a desired wrench on the Center of Mass (COM). This involved mapping contact forces to joint torques using the transpose of the Jacobian ($J^T$). To ensure physical feasibility, the optimizer enforced frictional cone constraints (no-slip) and unilateral constraints (no-pulling) at the feet. To ensure reliability, a PD fallback was implemented to take over whenever the solver (fmincon) failed to find a feasible solution within real-time limits.

Dynamic COM Stabilization

To enhance stability under heavy perturbations, I implemented a strategy to dynamically lower the desired Center of Mass. By commanding a downward trajectory, we effectively lowered the robot's profile and changed its effective rotational inertia, which proved crucial for rejecting larger external torques. This lowered configuration allowed the force-controller to more effectively distribute weight across the contact points, leading to a much higher survival time against random pushes and reaching our top score.

Performance Analysis & Results

Through iterative testing, our team, "Gain of Thrones," achieved a competitive score of 239.96. We explored the trade-offs between different solver configurations and discovered that small modeling choices, such as the convention used for state rotations, had a massive impact on the controller's ability to interpret the robot's orientation correctly. We also analyzed the impact of "ghost" contact points, adjusting force-control gains algorithmically when feet were not fully grounded to prevent unstable oscillations.

Demonstration of the control stack achieving stable stepping.

projects.name: Dynamic Simulation and Control of a Jumping Leg
projects.title: Robotics & Controls Developer
projects.tldr:
• Built a complete MATLAB hybrid simulation for a 3-DOF robotic leg, modeling stance, flight, and impact dynamics.
  • Symbolically derived the complete Lagrangian dynamics and implemented event functions for takeoff (event_takeoff.m) and touchdown.
  • Designed a virtual constraint-based controller (dynamics_stabilize.m) to stabilize the leg's posture and reject external forces.
  • Generated smooth 5th-order polynomial trajectories (desired_jump_trajectory.m) for the Center of Mass (COM) to achieve stable vertical jumps.
  • Extended the COM tracking controller to simulate dynamic forward and backward leaps, preparing the code for hardware implementation.
projects.summary:
This project involved developing the complete dynamic simulation and control stack for a 3-DOF robotic leg. The goal was to build a controller that could first stabilize the leg, then execute a controlled vertical jump, and finally perform a dynamic leap. I used MATLAB's Symbolic Toolbox to derive the system's dynamics (generate_files.m), built a hybrid event-driven simulation (simulate_jumping_leg.m), and designed multiple controllers to achieve this behavior.

Hybrid Dynamic Modeling

I began by symbolically deriving the full Lagrangian dynamics (D, C, G matrices) and kinematics. The system was modeled as a hybrid system with three distinct phases: Flight (standard ballistic dynamics, dynamics_flight.m), Impact (a discrete, inelastic collision map, dynamics_impact.m), and Stance (a constrained system, dynamics_stance.m). Event functions for takeoff and touchdown were written to manage the transitions between these states.



Stabilization & Force Rejection

Before jumping, the leg needed to be able to stand. we implemented a virtual constraint-based controller (dynamics_stabilize.m) to enforce a desired standing posture. This controller proved robust, as it could actively reject external forces and reliably return the leg to its stable configuration while adhering to physical constraints like no-liftoff and no-slip.



Vertical Jump & COM Trajectory

To achieve a jump, I designed a desired trajectory for the leg's Center of Mass (COM) using 5th-order quintic polynomials in desired_jump_trajectory.m. This ensures a smooth path with continuous position, velocity, and acceleration. I then implemented a COM tracking controller in the stance phase (dynamics_stance.m) to follow this path, squatting to build potential energy and then extending to execute a stable vertical jump and controlled landing.



Dynamic Leaping & Hardware Prep

The final step was to generalize the COM tracking. By defining a 2D trajectory for the COM (e.g., moving forward *while* squatting and jumping), the same stance controller could be used to execute dynamic leaps. The simulate_jumping_leg.m script allows setting these horizontal takeoff parameters to simulate forward and backward leaps, validating the controller that is now ready for hardware implementation.

projects.name: Analysis, Control, and Optimization of a Three-Link Bipedal Walker
projects.title: Robotics & Controls Developer
projects.tldr:
• Derived the complete Lagrangian dynamics and built a high-fidelity hybrid simulation (swing/impact) for a three-link bipedal walker from first principles in MATLAB.
  • Modeled and validated real-world physical constraints, including ground reaction forces and friction cone limits, to successfully simulate passive dynamic walking.
  • Designed and implemented two distinct feedback control strategies—a PI velocity controller and a bio-inspired event-based state machine—to achieve stable walking on level ground.
  • Solved a complex nonlinear optimization problem using fmincon to find a mathematically-proven, stable, and periodic walking gait.
projects.summary:
This project was a comprehensive, first-principles investigation into bipedal locomotion. I individually developed the complete simulation and control pipeline for a three-link planar walker. Starting with only the robot's physical parameters, I derived its equations of motion, built a hybrid dynamics simulation, implemented feedback controllers, and ultimately solved for a stable, periodic walking gait using nonlinear optimization. All modeling, analysis, and simulation were conducted in MATLAB.

Dynamic Modeling & Simulation

I began by deriving the complete equations of motion from first principles using Lagrangian dynamics. This involved symbolically computing the Mass-Inertia Matrix D(q), Coriolis & Centripetal Matrix C(q, q̇), and Gravity Vector G(q). I then developed a hybrid dynamics model to accurately simulate walking, which accounted for both the continuous 'swing' phase and the instantaneous 'impact' event. This core simulation, built in MATLAB, served as the testbed for all subsequent control and optimization.



Physics-Based Validation

To validate the physical accuracy of my model, I first simulated passive dynamic walking (letting the robot walk down a slope powered only by gravity). This required implementing real-world constraints. I wrote checks to ensure the stance foot would not slip (by monitoring the friction cone limits, |Fst,x| ≤ μFst,y) and would not 'jump' (by ensuring positive vertical ground reaction force, Fst,y > 0). The successful passive simulation confirmed the model's fidelity.



Feedback Control Design

With a validated model, I developed two distinct feedback controllers to achieve stable walking on level groundI designed and tuned a PI controller to regulate the robot's average forward hip velocity to a target 0.5 m/s, demonstrating convergence over several steps.



Trajectory Optimization

The final phase of the project was to find a mathematically 'perfect' stride. We formulated this as a nonlinear constrained optimization problem to find a stable, periodic gait, solved using MATLAB's fmincon with an input-output linearizing controller. The objective function was to minimize the motor energy per distance traveled: J := (1 / x(TI)) ∫0TI ||u(t)||2 dt. This was solved subject to crucial physical constraints, including periodicity (the step state must repeat), a minimum average speed (x(TI) / TI ≥ vd), no-liftoff (Fst,y ≥ 0), and no-slip friction cone limits (|Fst,x| ≤ μFst,y). The successful convergence of the optimizer yielded a stable, efficient, and repeatable walking gait, completing the project's journey from first principles to a fully optimized solution.

projects.name: Passive Dynamic Two-Link Walker Simulation
projects.title: Robotics & Controls Analyst
projects.tldr:
• Developed a complete MATLAB simulation for a two-link passive walker ('compass gait') using ode45 to solve the continuous-time dynamics.
  • Modeled the hybrid nature of walking by implementing a discrete impact map to calculate the state change during the foot-strike event.
  • Chained the continuous and discrete dynamics together to simulate 10 complete, continuous steps of the walker descending a slope.
  • Analyzed the gait's stability by numerically computing the Poincaré map and linearizing it to find the eigenvalues of the gait's fixed point.
projects.summary:
This project was a foundational study in passive dynamic locomotion. I built a hybrid simulation from the ground up in MATLAB to model a two-link walker (the 'compass gait' walker) descending a gentle slope, powered only by gravity. This involved deriving and implementing both the continuous 'swing' dynamics and the discrete 'impact' event. The project culminated in a formal stability analysis of the resulting gait using a Poincaré map.

Hybrid Dynamics Simulation

The core of the project was building a robust hybrid simulation. I first implemented the continuous dynamics in a two_link_dynamics.m function, which provided the time-derivative of the state (using the given equations of motion) to be solved by MATLAB's ode45. Next, I created a two_link_impact.m function to model the inelastic collision of the swing foot with the ground, which algebraically calculates the post-impact state from the pre-impact state. Finally, I combined these into a two_link_step.m function that simulates one full step and successfully chained 10 steps together, as seen in the animation.



Gait Stability Analysis (Poincaré Map)

To formally analyze the stability of the passive gait, I implemented a Poincaré map. I wrote a MATLAB function TwoLinkPoincare.m that takes a state on the Poincaré section (defined by the foot-strike event) and simulates one full step, returning the state at the next foot-strike. By linearizing this map around its fixed point, I computed the Jacobian (A) of the map. The eigenvalues of A determine the local stability of the periodic orbit, completing the analysis of the passive walker's gait.

projects.name: Teleoperation of Kuka Robotic Arm
projects.title: Software Engineer
projects.tldr:
• Led a team of three in developing a VR system for teleoperating a KUKA robotic arm with hand-tracking and a two-finger haptic feedback glove, improving user control and precision.
  • Designed, manufactured and tested the haptic glove, developed electrical schematics, and wrote Python scripts for two-way communication with the robotic arm.
  • Developed software for real-time robotic arm control, integrating the Robotiq Gripper 2F-140, Unity-based control system, and OPC UA communication.
  • Sourced and implemented cameras (Zed, RealSense, and LogiCamera) to enhance immersive teleoperation with a Xavier Jetson.
  • Led project administration, including team formation, ethics approval, risk assessments, and project planning.
projects.summary:
I led a team of three in developing an integrated virtual reality system designed to enhance user control and precision in teleoperating robotic arms. This system, implemented in the Monash Smart Manufacturing Hub's Digital Twin Lab, enables intuitive real-time manipulation of a KUKA robotic arm using VR hand-tracking and an advanced two-finger haptic feedback glove. Working every day for three months over the summer, we achieved significant milestones.

Haptic Glove

I designed and tested seven iterations of the glove, sourced components, created the electrical schematic, soldered and crimped connections, and wrote Python scripts on a Raspberry Pi Model 4B to enable two-way communication with the robotic arm gripper. Additionally, I designed the housing for the Raspberry Pi. The haptic glove now functions seamlessly upon power-up.



Robotic Arm

I wrote the KUKA Sunrise Java code that allows the robotic arm and end effector to receive values from the server, enabling real-time control. This required an in-depth understanding of OPC UA to create new variables, as well as extensive research into KUKA Sunrise and Robotiq Gripper 2F-140 documentation. Ultimately, I successfully integrated the gripper with both the KUKA robotic arm and the server.

VR & Hand Tracking

I developed the virtual lab environment that users interact with in VR. Additionally, I wrote C# scripts that track the user's hand, calculate movement differences, and transmit the data to the server for the robotic arm to mimic. I also wrote scripts for mapping gripper movement in Unity and learned how to integrate different robotic frames. Furthermore, I co-wrote the locomotion scripts that allow users to navigate the lab and authored the view-changer script, which lets users switch between different perspectives.



Camera Streams

I sourced and implemented a Zed Camera, RealSense Camera, and LogiCamera, integrating them with a Xavier Jetson to enhance teleoperation by making control more immersive and intuitive.



Software Development

My contributions extended to software development, where I wrote the code that connects the KUKA robotic arm to the server, implemented OPC UA for industrial communication, and developed the Unity-based control system for the gripper. Additionally, I engineered the hand-tracking system, calculated movement differences, and transmitted them to the server while integrating all camera streams for a seamless operator experience.

Administration

I formed and led the team, holding weekly meetings with our supervisor and bi-weekly meetings with the team. I also wrote all the necessary documentation to obtain ethics approval, including the Explanatory Statement, Consent Form, Interview Topics, and Survey Questions - ensuring we could conduct testing with participants. Additionally, I authored and secured approval for two detailed risk assessments, one for the project as a whole and another specifically for the full-body haptic suit, assuming the role of Risk Owner. I conducted extensive academic research in this field, developed a six-month project timeline (Gantt Chart), and contributed significantly to the project report.



Ultimately, this project was highly rewarding. By reducing cognitive strain and improving operational accuracy, we laid the groundwork for future advancements in haptic-enhanced teleoperation.

projects.name: Autonomous Driving
projects.title: ML Engineer
projects.tldr:
• Developed an autonomous delivery robot capable of navigating both urban and rural Australian roads using deep learning for real-time steering commands, and secured 1st place in the Need4Speed Challenge at RVSS 2025.
  • Collected and labeled 3,000 images to train the model, applying various data augmentation techniques for improved robustness.
  • Trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict seven distinct steering commands with ~75% accuracy, and incorporated stop sign detection using color thresholding.
  • Implemented dynamic speed control based on road conditions, ensuring optimal performance in both straight and curved roads.
  • For more information, visit the GitHub page.
projects.summary: I developed a convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict vehicle steering for autonomous driving, enabling my robot to navigate both urban and rural roads. The model processed RGB camera images to generate real-time steering commands, incorporated stop sign detection, and dynamically adjusted speed based on road conditions. After extensive data collection, training, and deployment on a Raspberry Pi-controlled robot, I secured 1st place in the Need4Speed Challenge at RVSS 2025, demonstrating exceptional performance in autonomous navigation and real-world adaptability.
